column2: with lips like bimba fruit, their mouths reddened and shining with betel, wearing gold ornaments and adorned with every decoration,
youthful and fair, with lovely hips, sounding with girdles and anklets, wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes,
clever, fortunate, lovely, graceful in limb and pleasing to see, endowed with beauty and charm, all with smiling faces.
Playing, intoxicated with delight, in halls and squares, those women give pleasure with song, music, stories and conversation.
Chief courtesans are seen, skilled in dance and song, clever in glances and talk, endowed with all feminine accomplishments.
Other women are seen there too — noble ladies who are teachers of virtue, devoted to their husbands, fortunate and adorned with every virtue.
With holy woods and groves, charming gardens and divine temples beautiful with various flowers,
with shalas, palmyras, tamalas, bakulas, nagakesaras, pippalas, karnikaras, sandal, aloe and champakas,
punnagas, coconuts, jackfruits, sarala trees, oranges, lakuchas, lodhras, saptaparnas and shubhanjanas,
mangoes, bilvas, kadambas, shimshapas, dhavas, khadiras, patalas, ashokas, tagaras and karaviras red and white,
yellow arjunas, bhallatakas, siddhas and amratakas, banyans, ashvatthas, kashmaryas, palashas and devadarus,
mandaras, parijatas, tamarinds, vibhitakas, prachina-amalakas, plakshas, jambus and shirisha trees,
kaleyas, kanchanaras, madhujambiras, tindukas, date palms, agastyas, bakulas, shakhotakas and haritakis,
kankolas, muchukundas, hintalas, citrons, groves of ketaki, atimuktas and kubjakas,
mallika, kunda and bana flowers, adorned with clusters of plantains, matulungas, areca palms, karunas and sinduvaras,
bahuvaras, kovidaras, badaras, karanjakas, and other various flowering trees and other charming ones,
with creepers, shrubs and canopies, gardens like Nandana, always rich with the scent of flowers and always bent with loads of fruit,
delightful with the cries of various birds, filled with herds of various beasts, with chakoras, shatapatras, bhringaras and priyaputrakas,
sparrows, peacocks, parrots and cuckoos, doves, wagtails, hawks and pigeons,
and other birds of many kinds, pleasant to the ear and charming; rivers, lotus pools and very many lakes,
and other holy reservoirs adorned with water-lilies and lotuses, red and white lotuses and fragrant kahlaras,
and other various very charming water-born flowers, divine, spreading fragrance, bright with the blossoms of every season,
crowded with swans and karandavas, beautiful with chakravakas, with cranes, herons, tortoises, fish and crocodiles,
with jalapadas, kadambas, plavas and water-fowl, and other birds and aquatic creatures adorned with various cries,
of various colours and always joyful, filling it all around. Thus with various flowers and various reservoirs,
with various holy trees and various gardens, with creatures of water and land and birds dwelling in lovely places,
and with divine temples, that great city was beautiful. There dwells the Lord, the god, the three-eyed enemy of Tripura,
famed as Mahakala, Shiva who grants all desires. A man who bathes duly in the Shivakunda, destroyer of sin,
the wise one, having duly satisfied the gods, ancestors and sages, then goes to Shiva's temple and circumambulates it three times;
entering, self-restrained, in washed garments and with senses controlled, with baths, flowers, perfumes, incense and lamps, with devotion,
with food offerings and presents, with song, music and circumambulation, with prostrations like a staff, dances and hymns to Shankara —
having worshipped Mahakala Shiva duly with devotion even once, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices.
Freed from all sins, mounting celestial cars that fulfil every wish, he goes to heaven where Shambhu's abode is.
Bearing a divine form, glorious, adorned with divine ornaments, he enjoys excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of beings.
In Shiva's world, O best of sages, free from old age and death; when his merit is exhausted he comes here and is born in an excellent brahmin family,
a brahmin learned in the four Vedas and skilled in all scriptures; having attained the Pashupata yoga, he then attains liberation.
There flows the holy river famed by the name Shipra; bathing in it duly and satisfying the ancestors and deities,
freed from all sins and mounted on an excellent celestial car, the best of men enjoys many kinds of pleasures in the world of heaven.
There too dwells the Lord Janardana, god of gods, named Govindasvamin — Hari, giver of enjoyment and liberation.
Seeing him, one attains liberation together with twenty-one generations; in a celestial car coloured like the sun, hung with networks of bells,
rich in every desire, moving at will and restless, sung to by Gandharvas, he is honoured in Vishnu's world,
and enjoys various desires, free from fear and fever, until the dissolution of beings, handsome, fortunate and happy.
In due time returning, the wise one becomes a brahmin on earth in an excellent house of yogins, knowing the truth of the Vedas and scriptures,
and having taken up the yoga of Vishnu, he then attains liberation. Seeing Vishnu named Vikramasvamin there, O brahmins,
man or woman obtains the fruit described before. Other gods led by Shakra dwell there too,
and the Mothers, O best of sages, granting the fruit of every desire; seeing them, worshipping them duly with devotion and bowing,
a man freed from all sins goes to heaven. Thus that delightful city was protected by the lion among kings,
joyful with constant festivals like Indra's Amaravati, joined with eighteen suburbs, with very broad crossroads,
resounding with the twang of bowstrings, adorned with gatherings of Siddhas, abounding in groups of learned men, resounding with the recitation of the Vedas.
Itihasas, Puranas, various scriptures, poetry, conversations and stories are heard there day and night, O brahmins.
Thus I have described that city rich in virtues, in which formerly lived the great-minded King Indradyumna.
Elephant-doctors, physicians, doctors of men, tree-doctors, cattle-doctors and others who cut and cauterise —
all these citizens, and others not mentioned, all the inhabitants of the city followed the king,
as eager sons follow their father when he goes to another village, so those citizens followed him.
Thus that glorious king, surrounded by all the great people, with elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers, went slowly on.
Having thus gone, followed by all those forces for a long time, the lord king reached the shore of the southern ocean.
He saw the delightful ocean, standing as if dancing, crowded with many hundreds of thousands of waves,
full, the abode of various gems, teeming with various creatures, abounding in ripples and waves, filled with great wonders,
the king of holy places, roaring loudly, boundless and very terrifying, like a mass of clouds, fathomless, the abode of makaras,
filled with fish, tortoises, conches, oysters, crocodiles and shankus, with porpoises and crabs and serpents of great venom,
the salt ocean, Hari's place of rest, lord of rivers, destroyer of all sins, holy, granting the fruit of every wish,
deep with many whirlpools, refuge of the Danavas, the divine churning-source of nectar, source of the gods, lord of waters,
distinguished among all beings, sustainer of the lives of creatures, purest of the pure, most auspicious of the auspicious,
best of holy places, imperishable, lord of aquatic creatures, whose measure is established like the waxing and waning of the moon,
impenetrable to all beings, abode of the gods' nectar, the eternal cause of origin, sustenance and dissolution,
the support of all, holy lord of rivers and streams — seeing him, the best of kings was filled with supreme wonder.
He made his dwelling there, reaching the shore of the ocean, in a holy and charming land endowed with every quality of good ground,
surrounded by shalas, kadambas, punnagas, sarala trees, jackfruits, coconuts, bakulas and nagakesaras,
palmyras, pippalas, date palms, oranges, citrons, shalas, amratakas, lodhras, bakulas and bahuvarakas,
kapitthas, karnikaras, patalas, ashokas, champakas, pomegranates, tamalas, parijatas and arjunas,
prachina-amalakas, bilvas, priyangus, banyans, khadiras, ingudis, saptaparnas, ashvatthas, agastyas and jambus,
madhukas, karnikaras, bahuvaras, tindukas, palashas, badaras, nipas, siddhas, nimbas and shubhanjanas,
varakas, kovidaras, bhallatakas and amalakas, hintalas, ankolas, karanjas and vibhitakas,
sarjas, madhukas, kashmaryas, shalmalis, devadarus, shakhotakas, nimbas, banyans, kumbhis, kaushthas and haritakis,
guggulus, sandal trees, aloe and patalas, jambira and karuna trees, tamarinds and red sandal —
thus with trees of various kinds and many other trees, with wish-fulfilling trees ever in fruit and masses of flowers of every season,
divine with the cries of various birds, resounding with intoxicated cuckoos, echoing with fine peacocks, crowded with parrots and mynahs,
with haritas, bhringarajas, chatakas, bahuputrakas, jivanjivakas, kakolas, sparrows and doves,
and other birds of various kinds, pleasant to the ear and charming, singing from lovely perches on the flowering tops of trees,
with groves of ketaki always bearing white flowers, mallika and kunda blossoms, yuthikas and tagaras,
kutajas, bana flowers, atimuktas and kubjakas, malatis, karaviras and golden plantains,
and other flowers of various kinds, fragrant and lovely to see, born in woods, gardens and groves, of various colours and fragrant,
crowded with hosts of Vidyadharas, frequented by Siddhas and Charanas, by Gandharvas, serpents and Rakshasas, spirits, Apsarases and Kinnaras,
crowded with hosts of sages and Yakshas, frequented by various creatures, with deer, monkeys and lions, full of boars and buffaloes,
and other deer such as black bucks, beautiful everywhere, with tigers, blazing elephants and other forest-dwellers.
Thus with various trees and gardens like Nandana, canopies of creepers and shrubs and various reservoirs,
crowded with swans and karandavas, adorned with clusters of lotuses, with kadambas, plavas and swans, beautiful with chakravakas,
with lotuses, hundred-petalled lotuses, kahlaras, water-lilies and blue lotuses, birds, aquatic creatures and flowers born of water,
with mountains with blazing peaks, adorned with lovely caves, covered with various trees and adorned with various minerals,
with peaks full of every wonder, auspicious abodes of all beings, rich in all herbs, with vast and variegated slopes —
thus that king saw a place adorned with all these charming things together, worshipped by the three worlds,
ten yojanas wide and five yojanas long, filled with various wonders, a most rare region.
All this was darkness, and nothing could be discerned. In it keeps watch the Self of beings, the Supreme Self, the teacher of the world,
the glorious god who makes the three forms, maker of the world, the great Lord, famed as Vasudeva, whose self is yoga, Hari the Lord.
At the end of his yogic sleep he created, seated in the middle of the lotus of his navel, Brahma, like the filaments of a lotus, the imperishable being.
Then Brahma, great lord of all the worlds, being thus, slowly creates what is joined with the five elements —
beings arising from the subtle elements, gross and subtle, all four kinds, unmoving and moving.
Then Brahma, lord of creatures, made all the moving and unmoving; reflecting on himself with his mind, he created various creatures:
all the sages led by Marichi, gods, Asuras and ancestors, Yakshas, Vidyadharas and others, and the rivers beginning with the Ganga,
men, monkeys and lions and various birds, the womb-born, the egg-born, O Goddess, the sweat-born and the sprout-born,
the fourfold brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra, and the lowest castes and barbarians — he created them separately in their variety.
Whatever is called a living being, down to grass, shrubs and ants — becoming Brahma, he fashioned the whole world, moving and unmoving.
Contemplating himself as a man on the right side and a woman on the left, he made himself twofold.
From then on creatures in this world are born of sexual union — the low, the high and the middle, and whatever are my regions.
Having reflected thus, long ago, the water-born god went into meditation on the body whose self is Vasudeva.
By the god's mere meditation, Janardana himself arose at that moment — thousand-eyed, thousand-footed,
the thousand-headed Person, with eyes like white lotuses, like a dark cloud over the waters, glorious, marked with the Shrivatsa.
Brahma, grandsire of the worlds, suddenly saw him and, welcoming him with seats, water for the feet and hands, and unbroken rice,
Virinchi, well composed, praised him with supreme hymns. Then I said to the god Brahma, born of the lotus: "Tell me, dear one, the reason for your meditation now."

For the good of the world, lord of gods — the paths to heaven's gate, hard for the mortal world to reach, sacrifices, gifts and vows,
brahmapuran:45:45	yoga, truth, austerity, faith and various holy places — leaving all these aside, tell me an easy means to it.
brahmapuran:45:46	O lord of the world, tell me the place that is called most excellent on earth, the best place of all, O Purushottama.
Hearing the Creator's words, my dear, I then said: "Listen, Brahman, I shall tell you of a pure place, rare on earth,
the best of all regions, blessed, carrying one across worldly existence, beneficial to cows and brahmins, holy, bringing happiness to the four classes,
granting enjoyment and liberation to men, a most rare region, of great merit, granting perfection to all, O Grandsire.
From it arose the eternal king of holy places, the famed supreme region, frequented in all four ages.
Of all the gods, sages and celibates, Daityas, Danavas and Siddhas, Gandharvas, serpents and Rakshasas,
Nagas and Vidyadharas, the unmoving and the moving — because he is the supreme Person, therefore he is Purushottama.
On the shore of the southern ocean, where the banyan tree stands, is a most rare region ten yojanas wide.
When a kalpa arises with the destruction of great meteors, it does not perish, for I myself abide there thus.
By merely seeing that banyan and stepping into its shade repeatedly, one is freed from the sin of brahmin-slaying — what then of other sins?
Those creatures who circumambulate it and bow to it are all freed from sin and go to the abode of Keshava.
A little to the north of the banyan and to the south of Keshava stands a temple there; that is a place made of dharma.
Seeing the image there, made by the god himself, men then go effortlessly to my world."
Seeing them going, my dear, one day the king of dharma came near me, bowed his head and said:

Salutation to you, O Lord, god, lord of the worlds, master of the universe, the god who dwells in the milk ocean and lies on the coils of Shesha,
brahmapuran:45:61	the best, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the maker, the unmade, the Lord, master of the universe, unborn Vishnu, all-knowing and unconquered,
brahmapuran:45:62	dark as a blue lotus petal, with eyes like white lotuses, all-knowing, without qualities, tranquil, the imperishable sustainer of the world,
brahmapuran:45:63	ordainer of all worlds, bringer of happiness to all worlds, the ancient Person to be known, manifest and unmanifest, eternal,
brahmapuran:45:64	creator of the high and the low, lord of the world, teacher of the world, marked with the Shrivatsa on his chest and adorned with the forest garland,
brahmapuran:45:65	clad in yellow, four-armed, bearing conch, discus and mace, with necklace and armlets, wearing crown and bracelets,
brahmapuran:45:66	complete with every good mark, free of all senses, unchanging, immovable, subtle, of the form of light, eternal,
brahmapuran:45:67	free from being and non-being, all-pervading, beyond Prakriti — I bow to the Lord of the world, the Lord who grants happiness, the Master.
Thus long ago the king of dharma, near the banyan, praised him with various hymns and then bowed.
Seeing him bowing with joined palms, O illustrious Goddess, I asked the Ender the reason for his hymn:
O mighty-armed son of Vivasvan, you are foremost among all the gods; why did you praise me? Tell me that briefly.

In this holy shrine, the famed Purushottama, there is an excellent image made of sapphire that fulfils every desire.
brahmapuran:45:72	Seeing it with single-minded devotion and faith, O lotus-eyed one, even men without desires go to the abode called Shveta.
brahmapuran:45:73	Therefore I cannot carry out my work, O slayer of foes. Be gracious, great god, and withdraw the image, O Lord.
Hearing these words of the son of Vivasvan, he said this: "Yama, I will hide it all around with sand."
Then, O Goddess, that image was hidden by me with creepers, so that men seeking heaven do not see it there.
Having covered it, O Goddess, with creepers and golden coverings, I sent Yama back to his own city in the southern direction.
When the sapphire image had vanished, O brahmins, in that holy excellent region, the famed Purushottama,
whatever events took place there, Janardana, god of gods, the Lord, told her all of it long ago:
the coming of Indradyumna, his seeing of the region, the description of the region, and the building of the temple,
the performance of the horse sacrifice, the seeing of the dream, the finding of the log on the shore of the salt ocean,
the appearance of Vasudeva and the king of craftsmen, O brahmins, and the fashioning of the images, each according to its colour,
the installation of all of them in the finest temple in the world, and at the time of the festival, O best of brahmins, the recounting of the kalpa,
the story of Markandeya and the installation of Shankara, the greatness of the Panchatirtha and the seeing of the trident-bearer,
the seeing of the banyan and its glory, O brahmins, and especially the seeing of Baladeva and Krishna,
and of Subhadra there and her greatness in full, the seeing of Narasimha and the recounting of his glory,
the seeing of Ananta Vasudeva and the praise of his virtues, the greatness of Shveta Madhava and the seeing of the gate of heaven,
the seeing of the ocean, bathing and libations, the greatness of bathing in the sea and of Indradyumna, O brahmins,
the fruit of the Panchatirtha and of the Mahajyeshtha, the abode of Krishna and the plough-bearer, and the fruit of festival pilgrimages,
the description of Vishnu's world and of the region again and again — all this Purushottama told her long ago.
going into the womb of the southern ocean, very beautiful with its whirlpools, on both of whose banks villages and towns
are seen, O tigers among sages, rich in crops and very charming, crowded with happy, well-fed people adorned with clothes and ornaments.
Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras are seen there, each devoted to his own dharma, peaceful and with auspicious marks.
Their mouths full of betel, adorned with garlands; the brahmins' mouths full of the Vedas with the six limbs and the pada and krama recitations,
some devoted to the Agnihotra, some to domestic fire rites, skilled in the meaning of all scriptures, sacrificers with abundant fees.
In squares, on royal roads, in woods and groves, in assembly halls, pavilions and mansions, and in temples,
the Itihasas and Puranas, the Vedas with their limbs well recited, poetry, scriptures and stories are heard there among the great people.
The women dwelling in that land are proud of beauty and youth, endowed with every good mark, with broad hips,
lotus-faced, youthful, with faces like the autumn moon, all with full, raised breasts, lovely to see in their prosperity,
wearing golden bracelets, adorned with divine garments, like the inner stem of the plantain, with the lustre of lotus filaments,
with lips like bimba fruit, lovely, with eyes reaching to their ears, fair-faced and with lovely hair, bent with grace and coquetry.
Some have eyes like lotus petals, some like blue lotuses, some with teeth bright as lightning, others slender of limb,
with curling locks, shining with the parting of their hair, wearing neck ornaments and adorned with garlands,
with jewelled earrings and charming ear-ornaments, like the women of the gods — women with auspicious marks are seen.
The lovely women play with excellent divine songs, with lutes, flutes, drums, panavas and gomukhas,
with the sounds of conches and kettledrums and various charming instruments; those playful women always play happily with one another.
Thus, skilled in many songs and instruments, the lovely women, intoxicated with love, are engaged day and night.
It is frequented by mendicants, Vaikhanasas, Siddhas, graduates and celibate students, and by those perfected in mantra, austerity and sacrifice.
Thus the king saw that supremely beautiful region: "Right here I shall worship the eternal Lord,
the teacher of the world, the supreme god, the supreme shore, the supreme state, Vishnu, lord of the lords of all, endless and unconquered.
This is that holy place of the mind, known to me as Purushottama, where the huge wish-fulfilling banyan tree stands.
The sapphire image has been hidden by the god himself, and no other auspicious image of Vishnu is seen here.
So I shall strive so that the god, lord of the world, Vishnu of true valour, comes before my eyes.
With sacrifices, gifts, austerities, fire offerings, meditations, worship and fasts, I shall duly observe the supreme vow.
With a single mind, absorbed in him and thinking of nothing else, I shall begin the construction of a temple of Vishnu."
With elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers, with ministers and family priests, come all together at the command of Indradyumna.
Thus instructed by that great-souled king, the messengers went and told the kings the words of that ruler.
Hearing the words of the messengers, all those kings came quickly, surrounded by their own armies —
kings from every quarter, those in the south, those in the west and those in the northern lands,
those dwelling on the borders and those dwelling near, those of the mountains and those dwelling on islands —
with chariots, elephants, foot soldiers, horses and abundant wealth, many arrived, O brahmins, having heard Indradyumna's command.
Seeing those kings arrive with their ministers and family priests, the king, glad at heart, respectfully spoke about the task:

Listen, O tigers among kings, to what I have to say. In this excellent, holy, auspicious region that grants enjoyment and liberation,
brahmapuran:47:20	how can I perform the great horse sacrifice and build a temple of Vishnu? — so my mind is troubled with anxiety.
brahmapuran:47:21	With you as good helpers I will accomplish all this, if you will be my helpers, O best of kings.
As the wise king of kings spoke thus, all those kings were delighted and glad at his command.
They showered wealth and gems, gold, jewels and pearls, blankets, skins and gems, and fine deer-wool coverings,
diamonds, beryl, rubies, padmaragas and sapphires, elephants, horses and other wealth, chariots and female elephants,
countless materials of many kinds, high and low, shali rice, paddy and barley, beans, green gram and sesame,
mustard and chickpeas, wheat, lentils and the like, shyamaka millet, madhuka, wild rice and horse-gram,
and other various grains, cultivated and wild, in thousands, with heaps of many thousands of grains and rice,
pots of cow's ghee by hundreds and thousands, and other various materials, foods to chew and eat, and unguents —
the kings filled it with whatever materials there were. Seeing those sacrificial materials endowed with every wealth,
and the brahmins who knew the rites of sacrifice, masters of the Vedas and their limbs, expert in the scriptures, capable and skilled in all rites,
the seers, great seers, divine seers and ascetics, celibates, householders, forest-dwellers and renunciants,
graduates and other brahmins ever engaged in the Agnihotra, excellent teachers and preceptors endowed with study and austerity,
members of the assembly skilled in the scriptures and many other purifiers — seeing them, the glorious king said to his family priest:
Let the learned brahmins, masters of the Veda, go forth and find a place fit for sacrifice, to accomplish the horse sacrifice.
Thus addressed, the royal priest, glad, did as the king said, together with the ministers.
Then the wise priest went with the architects, placing in front the brahmins skilled in the rites of sacrifice.
In that place, the fishermen's village with its lanes and towers, the brahmin had the sacrificial enclosure made according to rule,
crowded with hundreds of mansions, beautiful with excellent gems, delightful like Indra's palace, adorned with gold and jewels.
Placing pillars painted with gold and great archways in the areas of the sacrificial halls, and pure gold,
the righteous one had inner apartments made for the kings dwelling in various lands, here and there according to rule.
For the brahmins and vaishyas who had come from various lands he had many halls made there according to rule.
To please that king, the best of kings came, bringing many gems, and women came to the festival.
As those great souls entered their own camps, a sound touching the sky arose, like the roaring of the ocean.
To those who had come, O best of sages, the king assigned dwellings and beds with due courtesy.
The best of kings himself approached and assigned various foods of shali rice, sugarcane, barley and milk products.
Likewise, at that great sacrifice, many expounders of Brahman and the foremost of the twice-born, O best of brahmins, who were there
came with their disciples; the king received them and accompanied them all as far as their lodgings,
the mighty best of kings himself, casting off pride. Then the craftsmen and others, having done their own work,
reported to the king the entire arrangement of the sacrifice. Hearing that all had been done, the tireless best of kings, Achyuta's devotee, thrilled with joy together with his ministers.
When that sacrifice began, eloquent debaters, desiring victory over one another, advanced many arguments.
It was arranged by that lion among kings like that of the lord of the gods, O brahmins; they saw archways made of gold,
many kinds of beds and seats, heaps of gems, pots, vessels, cauldrons, jars and vardhamanakas.
No king saw anything there that was not of gold. The sacrificial posts prescribed in the scriptures, of wood adorned with gold,
set up duly at the proper time, of great splendour; and all the animals, of land and water, O brahmins,
the kings saw brought there — cows, buffaloes and even old women,
aquatic creatures, beasts of prey and birds, the womb-born, egg-born, sweat-born and sprout-born,
and beings of the mountains and grain-fields — they saw them all. Thus, seeing everything delightful in animals, wealth and grain,
the kings who saw the sacrificial enclosure were filled with supreme wonder; for the brahmins and people there was much sweet food and abundance.
When a full hundred thousand brahmins had eaten there, a drum resounded again and again like the roar of clouds,
and it sounded repeatedly day after day. Thus the sacrifice of that wise king grew.
The brahmins saw very many heaps of food like mountains, streams of curd and lakes of milk.
The whole of Jambudvipa with its various countries, and brahmins too, were seen at that king's great sacrifice.
There thousands of men from here and there took vessels and went, many of them, O best of brahmins.
And all the attendants, wearing polished jewelled earrings, served the twice-born by hundreds and thousands.
The men who followed gave to the brahmins various drinks and foods fit for kings.
The generous king then duly honoured the knowers of the Veda who had come and the kings, lords of the earth,
the kings from all directions and lands, great in battle, actors, dancers and others skilled in song and praise.
His charming wives, with full, raised breasts, eyes like blue lotus petals and faces like the autumn moon,
endowed with lineage, character and virtue, numbered a thousand and one hundred. Thus, accompanied by that king's host of chief wives,
divine, full of jewelled garlands, served by banners and flags, delightful with jewelled necklaces, radiant like moonlight,
with mountain-like elephants, sprinkled with ichor, very mighty, in hundreds and crores, tuskers adorned with tusk-ornaments,
with horses swift as the wind, born in Sindhu, very beautiful, white horses with dark ears, in many crores, full of speed,
and with countless foot soldiers, armoured and girded, ready with various weapons, like sons of the gods —
thus the king saw the vast array of the sacrifice's provisions. Then the king was filled with joy and, delighted, said:

Bring the best horse, marked with every good sign, and let the well-disciplined princes let it roam over the earth.
brahmapuran:47:76	Let the fire offering be performed here by the learned and those who know dharma. Bring a black goat, a buffalo and a black buck, O twice-born,
brahmapuran:47:77	and an ox, cows and all the herdsmen. Let the sacrificial rites proceed, and then the temple of Vishnu.
brahmapuran:47:78	Let all this be given to the brahmins as they desire in their minds — women, crores of gems, villages and towns,
brahmapuran:47:79	well-endowed lands and territories for those who seek them, and many other charming kinds of goods.
brahmapuran:47:80	To all who ask, let 'there is none' never be said. Let the sacrifice go on until the god himself comes before my eyes here near this sacrifice.
Having said this, O brahmins, the mighty-armed lion among kings gave heaps of gold and crores of ornaments,
a hundred thousand female elephants, millions of horses, a hundred million bulls and cows with golden horns,
beautiful, fragrant, milk-rich cows with bronze milking-pails — these he gave joyfully to the brahmins who knew the Veda.
Very costly garments and deer-wool coverings, very white and bright, excellent coral and gems,
and various jewels he gave at the great sacrifice,
diamonds, beryl, rubies, pearls and the like; and adorned, fair maidens with lotus eyes,
five hundred, the joyful king gave to the brahmins — women with full breasts covered by bodices,

to the brahmins and other seekers at the horse sacrifice, O best of brahmins, and abundant food to chew and eat, joined with various provisions,
many sweets beginning with khandaka, steamed and cooked cakes, other pure foods, ghee-filled cakes and khandavas,
sweet fried cakes, well-cooked and tasty food; food was given again and again for the pleasure of all beings.
There was no end to the wealth given and being given. Seeing thus the great sacrifice, gods and Daityas with the Charanas,
Gandharvas and Apsarases, Siddhas, sages and lords of creatures were filled with supreme wonder at the sight of that excellent, auspicious rite.
The priest, the ministers and the king were delighted there in every way. There was no one unclean, wretched or hungry,
no calamity, no weariness, no mental or bodily ailment; there was no untimely death, no biting insect, no evil planet, no poison.
All the people were happy and well-fed at that king's great festival; and the sages perfected by austerity and long-lived who were there
said that no such sacrifice rich in wealth and grain had ever taken place. Thus, O best of brahmins, the king duly completed the horse sacrifice and likewise the temple of Vishnu.
The divisions called Sankarshana and the others, O Hari, have been told; they arose for your worship and therefore rest in you.
In ultimate truth there is no division in you, O lord of gods; whatever various forms of yours are spoken of are figurative.
How can a man speak of you, the non-dual, as dual? You alone, O Hari, are all-pervading, of the nature of consciousness, stainless.
Your supreme form is free of being and non-being, untainted, without qualities, the best, unchanging, immovable and fixed,
free of all limiting adjuncts, established as pure existence; even the gods do not know it — how can I, O Lord?
Your other form, clad in yellow, four-armed, holding conch, discus and mace, wearing crown and armlets,
marked with the Shrivatsa on the chest and adorned with the forest garland — that the gods worship, and others who take refuge in you.
O god of gods, best of the gods, giver of fearlessness to devotees, protect me, O lotus-eyed one, sunk in the ocean of sense-objects.
I see no other, O lord of the world, in whom I can take refuge, except you, O beloved of Kamala; be gracious, O Madhusudana.
Joined with hundreds of old age and diseases, oppressed by various sorrows, deluded by joy and grief, tightly bound by the fetters of karma,
I have fallen into the very fierce, terrible ocean of worldly existence, hard to cross with its bitter waters, full of the fish of attraction and aversion,
deep with the whirlpools of the senses, crowded with waves of craving and sorrow, without shelter, without support, without substance and exceedingly unstable.
Deluded by maya there, I have wandered a very long time, O Lord, born again and again in thousands of various species.
I have experienced many births, thousands and tens of thousands, of various kinds in this worldly existence, O Janardana.
I have studied the Vedas with their limbs and various scriptures, the Itihasas and Puranas and many crafts.
Discontents and contentments, gains, losses and expenses, O lord of the world, decay, growth and their opposites I have obtained.
Separations and unions with wife, enemies, friends and kinsmen; various fathers and mothers have been seen by me.
Sorrows have been experienced, and pleasures many times; kinsmen, sons, brothers and relatives have been obtained.
I have dwelt in women's wombs slimy with excrement and urine, and experienced the great sorrow of dwelling in the womb, O Lord.
The many sorrows that belong to childhood, youth and old age, O Hrishikesha, have been obtained by me.
The sorrows at death, on Yama's road and in Yama's abode, and the torments in hell, have been experienced by me.
In the wombs of worms, insects and trees, elephants, horses, deer and birds, buffaloes, camels, cows and other forest-dwellers,
of all the twice-born and of shudras, of the rich, of kshatriyas, of the poor and of ascetics,
of kings, of kings' servants and of other embodied beings — in their houses I have been born again and again, O god.
I have often gone into servitude to the servants of men, O Lord; I have gone to poverty, to lordship and to mastership.
I have been killed and I have killed others; I have been slain and others slain; others have given to me, and I have given to others many times.
For the sake of father, mother, friends, brothers and wife, to the rich, the learned, the poor and the ascetics,
I have spoken words of wretchedness of many kinds, abandoning shame, O Janardana. Among gods, animals and men, the unmoving and the moving,
there is no place where I have not gone, O Lord. Now I dwell in hell, now in heaven, O lord of the world,
now in the worlds of men, now among animals. As a pot bound by a rope on the wheel of a water-lift
goes up and down and sometimes stays in the middle, so I, O best of gods, covered by the rope of karma,
wander down, up and in the middle as it happens. Thus in this terrible, hair-raising wheel of worldly existence
I have wandered a very long time and never see an end. I do not know what to do today, O Hari, my senses in confusion.
